Leading PC makers are shifting some production back to China as costs bite. Firms including US-based HP â which had planned to shift more than half of its production out of the country in a âChina+1â strategy â are moving some manufacturing back to offset surging memory and storage chip prices fueled by AI demand.
Despite the risk of rising Western protectionism, experts believe more companies will return: â Chinaâs supply chain retains a distinct advantage ,â an analyst said.
Tech giants like Apple have sought to create alternative supply chains in India, which has spent billions to attract high-tech manufacturing. But âpaying its suppliers ever-larger subsidies in the hope of recreating China is unlikely to be a winning trade ,â a Bloomberg columnist argued.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft earnings live: Microsoft beats Q1 expectations on top and bottom line on AI growth
articles.title_zh: Microsoft earnings live: Microsoft beats Q1 expectations on top and bottom line on AI growth
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," the company's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
"We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options."
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
Pedro Sánchez says the government will act with urgency to ‘clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred’
At least 68 people have been killed after two passenger trains collided in Toledro province in central Spain, and the death toll may rise further.
A similar number of people remain hospitalised, including 15 in serious or critical state ( 15:44 ).
The two trains with 544 people on board in total ( 10:46 ) were travelling in the same direction on the high-speed line from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south-west of the country.
Video footage from the scene showed extensive damage to both trains ( 12:23 , 13:52 ).
Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said the country was “in mourning” as he insisted the government will get to the bottom of incident and address potential failures with “utmost firmness” ( 15:49 ).
Transport minister Óscar Puente said initial review of the evidence pointed to an “inexplicable” decision to order trains to go ahead after a signalling failure ( 15:01 ), implying a human error.
The investigation is likely to focus on 17 minutes between the trains were halted and the crash.
Spanish media reported that the controller responsible was questioned by investigators this afternoon ( 16:40 ).
Today’s collision is the second high-profile train crash in Spain this year ( 11:00 ), and the third deadliest incident on its railway in the last 50 years ( 12:55 ).
Spain is expected to declare three days of mourning later today ( 15:54 ).
Both main parties suspended their campaigning activities ahead of next month’s parliamentary election, but the far-right Vox party continued with its rallies ( 12:11 ).
At least 68 people have been killed and dozens more injured after two passenger trains collided in Toledro province in central Spain. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has declared three days of mourning in the wake of the disaster – the second high-profile train crash in Spain this year and the third deadliest incident on its railway in the last 50 years. Sánchez said his government would act with urgency to “clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred.”
The two trains with 544 people on board in total were travelling in the same direction on the high-speed line from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south-west of the country. One of the trains ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking several carriages off the track. Video footage from the scene showed extensive damage to both trains.
Sánchez insisted his government would get to the bottom of incident and address potential safety failures with “utmost firmness”. The government, he said, “must further strengthen safety to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail network”. He added: “This is essential, as it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to experience two high-speed rail accidents in a single year.”
Transport minister Óscar Puente said initial review of the evidence pointed to an “inexplicable” decision to order trains to go ahead after a signalling failure, implying a human error. The investigation is likely to focus on 17 minutes between the trains were halted and the crash. Spanish media reported that the controller responsible was questioned by investigators this afternoon. But, as my colleague Gwyn Topham wrote earlier , the Spanish public will want to know what led to the initial outage of a signalling system that was due to be phased out – and what circumstances or daily experience could have pressed someone to urge the trains to continue regardless, however tragically wrong that decision proved to be.
Both main parties suspended their campaigning activities ahead of next month’s parliamentary election, but the far-right Vox party continued with its rallies. Spain’s football federation also postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.
Thank you for following our live coverage. I’ll leave you with this report from our colleagues Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam.
The Health Department of Castilla-La Mancha has reduced the number of people in hospitals in the region to 53, after 56 were discharged, El Pais reported.
King Charles has contacted King Felipe of Spain .
The British monarch, who is currently out of the country visiting the Bahamas, “sent a private message of condolence” to his Spanish counterpart earlier today, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said.
The CSIF civil servants’ union has called for the resignation of Transport Minister Óscar Puente following Wednesday’s train accident.
“The minister is shamefully using a worker as a scapegoat instead of taking responsibility,” the union said, adding: “The minister has evaded all responsibility despite the initial computer system failure that triggered the events.
“Throughout this year, CSIF has demanded increased investment in the maintenance of the railway sector: safety, review and updating of safety protocols, and greater investment in infrastructure maintenance, as well as in railway workshops.”
Elsewhere, around twenty riot police officers are guarding the main entrance to the Ministry of Transport, the original location for a demonstration which was later moved to the neighboring Plaza de San Juan de la Cruz, El Mundo reported.
Spain’s Civil Guard said one of its officers, Jose Manuel, died in the train crash.
The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.
The number of people in hospital has risen to 107, The Emergency Services of Castilla-La Mancha said.
The president of the Andalusian Regional Government, Juanma Moreno, has demanded the central government conducts a “ complete review of the railway lines “ in Andalusia and in particular the high-speed line connecting the region with Madrid.
“The AVE high-speed train that links Madrid and Andalusia is no longer a safe means of transport,” Moreno added in comments reported by El Mundo.
Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.
“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.
Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.
“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”
The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash , in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.
Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain . Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.
As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.
Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.
A total of 36 people who were traveling on the trains involved in the Toledo train crash received medical attention at Atocha station, El Pais reported.

articles.title_orig: Cruise line folds over fuel costs, booting passengers in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Cruise line folds over fuel costs, booting passengers in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".
Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800.
Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.
There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.
The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.
"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."
"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."
Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."
Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.
Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia
During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.
In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package.
Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".
For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected.
"We loved our two years on Odysseyâthe adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way."
Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said.
The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter".
But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon.
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."
Additional reporting by Thanya Doksone.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | What China’s best new cultural spaces have in common: the light touch
articles.title_zh: Opinion | What China’s best new cultural spaces have in common: the light touch
articles.content_orig:
The cultural venues emerging in China today are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than those of recent decades
I served on the Frame Awards 2026 grand jury for the “institutions” categories. Three of the five projects shortlisted for the “cultural space” award were in mainland China: My Museum Beijing, Anji Hood and the Huishan Ancestral Hall Museum in Wuxi. China had 7,046 registered museums at the end of 2024, welcoming 1.49 billion visits that year.
Once a nation has built cultural venues on that scale, the question shifts from how many to what kind. The answers now emerging are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than the icons of recent decades.

articles.title_orig: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed Meeting Live Updates: Interest Rates Hold Steady Despite 'Elevated' Inflation
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues voted to hold their benchmark interest rate steady Wednesday. The central bank had raised rates in September, in an effort to curb persistent inflation. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America hide caption
The Federal Reserve opted not to raise interest rates Wednesday, but signaled that it's not retreating from the fight against stubborn inflation.
The central bank renewed its pledge to deliver price stability, a goal that's been made more difficult by a spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran.
"Inflation remains elevated," the Fed's rate-setting committee acknowledged in a statement .
At its last policy meeting in September, the Fed raised rates for the first time in more than three years. Since then, data has shown inflation has continued to accelerate, with consumer prices in September up 3.7% from a year ago — a bigger annual increase than the previous month.
"It's 'wrong way," says Dan North, a senior economist at the insurance company Allianz Trade. "That inflation line is going up, not down."
The decision not to adjust interest rates comes less than a week before votes are tallied in the midterm election, which may have contributed to the Fed's caution.
"It would be suspicious if there were a hike before the midterm," North said.
After a pause at this week's meeting, Fed policymakers are widely expected to raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December, in an effort to tamp down demand and bring prices under control.
Two members of the rate-setting committee wanted to move more quickly.  Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, while a majority of Fed policymakers opted to stand pat.
The Federal Reserve's benchmark rate — currently 3.75 to 4% — helps to establish the cost of other short-term lending for things like credit cards.
Longer-term interest rates are set by the bond market but can also be influenced by Fed decisions. Mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, before easing slightly. The high cost of home loans has been a drag on the housing market, which has been in a slump for the last four years.
Other parts of the economy are less sensitive to rising interest rates. The booming investment in artificial intelligence, for example, shows no sign of slowing down, no matter how much the Fed tries to tap on the brakes.
"The A.I. companies don't care what interest rate they have to pay," North says.
The frenzied push to build A.I. data centers is pushing up prices for construction materials and electronic equipment.
Consumer spending has also remained resilient, fueled in part by upper-income shoppers who benefit from the rising stock market.
That's not the case for less wealthy families, whose wages are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living. Average wages rose just 3% for the 12 months ending in September.
"Lower and middle-income Americans are having a real struggle," says Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.  " Their purchasing power is actually declining. And that's a pretty uncomfortable place to be. And that likely goes to explain to a large degree why people don't feel very good about the economy."

articles.title_orig: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.title_zh: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 5% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement .
Net income of $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, increased from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, in the same quarter of last year. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million impact from investing in OpenAI.
Free cash flow of $18.63 billion moved 27% lower. Cloud rival Alphabet showed negative free cash flow for the quarter, while Meta said last week that it went free cash flow negative .
Microsoft has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to accommodate artificial intelligence demand. The company had $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30%. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
For the first time in an earnings statement, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $32.32 billion, which would have represented growth of more than 44%. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments for the first time since 1998. For the past 11 years it had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
Agents and Infra gave Microsoft $76.80 billion of its revenue, which was up almost 25% and more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft cloud revenue beats estimates in sign that AI bet is paying off
articles.title_zh: Microsoft cloud revenue beats estimates in sign that AI bet is paying off
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," the company's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.title_zh: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.content_orig:
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.

articles.title_orig: Earnings live updates: ServiceNow stock plunges on Q3 earnings miss
articles.title_zh: Earnings live updates: ServiceNow stock plunges on Q3 earnings miss
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results dropping from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Read more: Follow Microsoft earnings live updates here.
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
ServiceNow ( NOW ) stock plunged 15% after the company missed earnings expectations.
Here's what the enterprise software company reported in Q3, versus analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: $4.1 billion, versus estimates of $4.09 billion
Earnings per share: $0.27, versus estimates of $0.35 per share
Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO): $13.65 billion, representing 20.5% year-over-year growth
Guidance: ServiceNow raised its forecast for 2026 subscription revenues to $15.78 billion to $15.79 billion.
"This was more than another beat-and-raise quarter for ServiceNow, this was the inflection point for ServiceNow as the Super Intelligence Control Tower," CEO Bill McDermott said in the earnings release. "Our customers have validated our strategic relevance as the single harness for enterprise intelligence and security."
Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) profit took a hit from an unusual place: its stakes in other companies.
Those holdings include about 14% of Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ). They supplied about $6 of Alphabet's $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter. In the third quarter, a nearly $9 billion loss on them cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12.
The filing that shows which stakes fell isn't out yet, but SpaceX stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Watch Anthropic's IPO, which could start trading as soon as Nov. 16. Once it's public, Alphabet will value that stake at the market price every quarter.
Chipotle ( CMG ) reported third quarter earnings on Wednesday after market close that were better than the Street expected as the restaurant chain sustained sales momentum following slower sales growth since the first quarter of 2025.
Chipotle posted a 2.1% gain in same-store sales, higher than the 1.5% gain Wall Street expected. It posted adjusted earnings of $0.27 per share, slightly below the $0.29 per share expected.
"Three consecutive quarters of positive comparable transaction growth demonstrates that our Recipe for Growth strategy is working," CEO Scott Boatwright wrote in the release, adding that the company saw traction around its menu and digital innovation, high-efficiency equipment rollout and global expansion.
The stock rose 2%. Year to date, shares are down 20%.
Yahoo Finance's Daniel Howley reports:
Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) reported its third quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, missing revenue projections on lower-than-anticipated advertising sales.
Google saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.12 on revenue of 127.58 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $3.01 on revenue of $127.93 billion. Revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs came in at $111.21 billion. Wall Street was anticipating $111.29 billion.
Google's advertising segment saw sales of $82.01 billion versus expectations of $83.5 billion, while its cloud unit brought in $30.71 billion. Analysts were projecting revenue of $29.1 billion.
The results come just hours after the company debuted its latest frontier AI model.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Ford ( F ) reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the end of the year.
For the quarter, Ford reported automotive revenue of $46.1 billion vs. $46.2 billion, per Bloomberg consensus, with adjusted EPS of $0.49 vs. $0.41, and adjusted EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $2.66 billion vs. $2.38 billion.
Ford tightened the low end of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to between $10.5 billion and $11 billion (from $10 billion to $11 billion seen prior); analysts projected full-year adjusted EBIT of $10.52 billion. Ford's adjusted free cash flow guidance remained at $6 billion to $7 billion.
Vertiv ( VRT ) stock surged 15% in premarket trading as the data center infrastructure player showed it continues to benefit from the massive capex spending from the likes of Google ( GOOG ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
"We are in the middle of the largest infrastructure buildout and it's accelerating," Vertiv's CEO Giordano Albertazzi said. "The demands on data center infrastructure are evolving faster than ever, and Vertiv's role in that buildout keeps expanding."
Vertiv makes power and cooling hardware for data centers and enterprise networks. As AI fuels demand for this infrastructure, Vertiv said its orders have doubled year over year. The company counts Alphabet, Microsoft, Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) among its customers, per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
That demand, plus strong third quarter results, have given Vertiv the confidence to raise its full-year outlook. In 2026, the company expects net sales of $14.45 billion to $14.85 billion, up from $13.8 billion to $14.2 billion.
Adjusted diluted earnings per share are expected to be $7.10-$7.20 for the year, representing earnings growth of 69%-71%. The midpoint of that range is above the $6.73 per share forecast Wall Street analysts penciled in.
In the third quarter, Vertiv reported net sales of $4.31 billion, beating Wall Street's expectations of $3.76 billion. Adjusted diluted earnings per share of $2.21 grew 78% year over year, also beating estimates of $1.82 per share.
Robinhood ( HOOD ) reported a weaker-than-expected third quarter profit on Tuesday as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the online brokerage despite record trading activity in stocks, options, and prediction markets.
The company reported net income of $476 million, down 14% from a year earlier, while diluted earnings per share fell 16% to $0.51. Revenue rose 12% to $1.42 billion. Analysts had expected earnings of $0.57 per share and revenue of $1.43 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
Robinhood stock fell 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday. The stock has slumped more than 15% since the start of 2026 through Tuesday's close, putting it on pace for its worst annual performance since 2022.
US-listed shares of SK Hynix ( SKHY ) rose 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday, after the memory maker's record profit and revenue quelled recent investor worries over the AI trade.
South Korean SK Hynix shares ( 000660.KS ) jumped 10% while peer Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) gained 5%. US-based Micron ( MU ) also rose 2%.
The South Korea-based company reported a 328% jump in quarterly revenue to roughly $78.7 billion, while operating profit surged 632% to about $62.7 billion, delivering an 80% operating margin. Revenue and operating profit increased by 32% and 38%, respectively, from the previous quarter.
Growth was driven by surging AI data center demand, higher memory prices, and early shipments of HBM4, which SK Hynix expects to replace HBM3E as its mainstream product.
United Parcel Service ( UPS ) stock rose 2% on Tuesday after the courier posted third quarter results and raised its full-year guidance, signaling solid demand during the upcoming holiday season.
Revenue is expected to come in at $92.6 billion this year, up from a prior forecast of $91.2 billion. UPS also increased its adjusted earnings guidance.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Quarterly Profit Soars as Cloud Growth Accelerates
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Quarterly Profit Soars as Cloud Growth Accelerates
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on a conference call with analysts. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wendy's ( WEN ) may be cooking up burgers for a billionaire soon.
Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant , according to an SEC filing.
Wendy's shares rose 15% in early trading. The company's market cap was $1.17 billion prior to the deal.
A Wendy's spokesperson didn't return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Trian Partners didn't return a request for comment.
Billionaire Peltz — while familiar with the operations — would essentially be buying a dumpster fire.
After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's is on the cusp of a large number of restaurant closures.
"With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a recent note.
"That said," he added, "given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system."
Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations. Reports emerged this week that it could close up to 60.
The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base.
Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills.
Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year.
There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US, and Barish estimated the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027.
The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations.
Wright officially took over as CEO on May 21, adding to the yawning list of executive turnover at the fast food chain over the past two years. He is a seasoned fast food exec who spent the previous five years fixing Potbelly as CEO. Wright's appointment marked a return to Wendy's, where he previously served in several senior leadership roles, including COO.
Wright has his work cut out for him in saving Wendy's beyond tightening up the store base count.
Wendy's has posted six straight quarters of same-store sales declines, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis.

articles.title_orig: Perv teacher learns fate for sex with 2 students — that already ended her job and marriage
articles.title_zh: Perv teacher learns fate for sex with 2 students — that already ended her job and marriage
articles.content_orig:
A married teacher in Australia was on Wednesday sentenced to just over a year in jail for having sex with two teenage students — which she tried to blame on “irresistible” impulses driven by bipolar disorder.
Tayla Lee Brailey , 32, wept as she hugged her parents and several supporters at her sentencing in Sydney on Wednesday — after already having lost her job and her husband after admitting her twisted crimes, Australian outlet ABC reported .
Brailey was first arrested in August 2024 for having sex with a 17-year-old boy in her car, returning to her classes after the sordid hookup.
She was released on bail — just to be busted again a few weeks later when it emerged she’d also touched a 16-year-old student’s genitals in her classroom, an experience that he said in a victim statement still overwhelms him with shame.
Brailey had groomed that younger victim online, according to the Canberra Times , sending him a naked picture of her in the shower and asking, “Do you like what you see?”
She then made him send her a nude in return. “Yum,” she replied to the 16-year-old student. “Stay back with me after school,” she wrote — with them kissing and touching each other’s genitals in her classroom.
“He has been feeling ashamed and had to leave high school before he finished … because of the shame he felt,” the judge, Justice Elizabeth Ryan, said during Bailey’s sentencing.
“He had suffered lack of sleep and flashbacks … he said none of his friends at high school speak to him anymore.”
The judge was told that Brailey was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder, creating impaired judgment and increased sex drive, leaving her with an “irresistible impulse” for sex with the boys, as the Australian also reported.
The judge, however, said that while Brailey’s crimes may have been “terrible mistakes,” she “used her position as a teacher … to abuse the trust of two young persons.”
“It is also relevant that she knew what she was doing was wrong but persisted with it,” Judge Ryan said.
“Offences like this cause immense harm to the trust that must exist between families and the education system,” the judge said.
“For these reasons … no penalty other than imprisonment is appropriate.”
Brailey was sentenced to nine months in prison for having sex with the 17-year-old student, and a year for sexually touching the 16-year-old boy, with an aggregate term of 15 months in jail.
She will also be placed on the child protection register for 15 years.
The teacher — who has since trained as an accountant — will be eligible for parole in April 2027.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Intel Warns China's Space-Based Directed Energy Weapons Could Soon Threaten Satellites
articles.title_zh: U.S. Intel Warns China's Space-Based Directed Energy Weapons Could Soon Threaten Satellites
articles.content_orig:
By the end of the decade, China could threaten satellites with space-based directed energy weapons, according to a new report from the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA). This would add a dangerous new anti-satellite (ASAT) capability to Beijing’s arsenal, which already includes ground-based directed energy weapons that can disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites. The report, released Monday, offered another glimpse into what is to come as the potential for conflict in space only continues to grow .
The unclassified DIA report is based largely on open-source information, with a cutoff date of July. It was published to detail growing threats from China, Russia and emerging powers Iran and North Korea to global interests in the space domain. The report’s release also took place as the U.S. is becoming increasingly open about its own ASAT capabilities. Last month, for instance, U.S. military officials acknowledged for the first time that America has weapons in orbit .
“The PLA probably considers DEWs [directed energy weapons] ideal counterspace systems because they can cause both reversible and nonreversible effects against satellites,” the report, titled Challenges to Security in Space , explains. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The report did not provide specifics about whether China is developing lasers, high-powered microwaves, particle beams or a combination of these capabilities.
We have reached out to the agency for more information but did not immediately receive a response.
Reversible attacks include efforts to jam satellite signals or temporarily blind their optics. The latter can be done with devices like laser dazzlers .
DIA reported that in 2021 the People’s Liberation Army media “asserted that laser weapons were entering a golden age; they cited dazzling (i.e., temporarily blinding a sensor) as one of the many operational uses of laser weapons.”
Non-reversible attacks cause permanent damage. It could also involve a range of fully destructive options from directed energy attacks that burn a hole in a satellite using a laser or frying its delicate systems using high-power microwave emissions, to spraying its solar panels with aerosol pigment, to direct-ascent intercepts and even nuclear weapon detonations in space . Physically tampering with the satellite using another satellite is another option.
China’s presence in orbit has been dramatically expanding in recent years. The report pointed out that as of July 2026, Beijing’s intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) satellite fleet “contained more than 510 systems, having more than tripled since 2018. While many of these ISR satellites are ostensibly affiliated with commercial and civil missions, the dual-use nature of their capabilities and possibly the Chinese military-civil fusion policies means the data or imagery they collect can be used by the PLA.”
China is also expanding its capabilities to new concepts like spaceplane developments, which we highlighted in a story about their capabilities yesterday based on details from the DIA report.
In addition to possibly being placed on satellites, DEWs could also potentially be added to spaceplanes, which can operate in a less predictable fashion than satellites, even if just for experimental roles or limited capability sets.
Though thin on details, the report reiterated the reality that China’s academia has been working toward space-based weapons for years.
“Since at least 2006, government-affiliated academics have investigated aerospace engineering technologies associated with space-based kinetic weapons—a class of weapon used to attack ground, sea, or air targets from orbit,” the DIA explained. “China’s space-based kinetic weapons research included methods of reentry, separation of payload, delivery vehicles, and transfer orbits for targeting purposes.”
Much of the PLA’s ASAT doctrine “characterizes the systems as useful deterrents against external involvement in a regional conflict or as a method to manage conflict escalation,” the DIA proffered. However, should China opt to strike first, one of the first and main targets would be satellites the U.S. and allies rely on for space-based sensing and communications. As we have often explained , even reversible attacks against any of this space-based infrastructure could have major impacts on the U.S. military’s ability to effectively conduct combat operations.
The DIA report noted that to date, China’s publicly known space-based ASAT capabilities center on satellites that can approach and grab others, which we have written about in the past . In one such instance, a Chinese satellite was observed in 2022 grabbing another satellite and pulling it out of its normal geosynchronous orbit and into a “super-graveyard drift orbit.” The maneuver raised questions about the potential applications of these types of satellites designed to maneuver close to other satellites for inspection or manipulation and added to growing concerns about China’s space program overall.
The threat satellites can already pose to others was highlighted earlier this month, when a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, may have passed within approximately 85 feet (26 meters) of ICEYE-X36. That is a U.S.-registered satellite belonging to commercial imagery provider ICEYE that was providing imagery to Ukraine. While no contact or damage was detected, the incident raised concerns that the Russian satellite could have harmed the ICEYE purposely or even inadvertently.
You can see a time-lapse video of part of that encounter below.
Short time-lapse of part of this morning’s first pass of ICEYE-X36 (59103) and COSMOS 2612 (68762) over South America under partly cloudy skies. pic.twitter.com/t8RhwmKcV4
When it comes to discussing weapons in space capable of attacking other on-orbit objects and the effects they could impose, it should be noted that this domain inherently creates complications when it comes to attributing any form of attack , should one occur. Satellites do malfunction, sometimes with catastrophic results, but it is not always possible to determine the cause. As a result, the challenge in attributing an event could delay a response, if needed, or spark one inadvertently.
As we previously reported , in January, “ a Russian inspector satellite launched in 2014 appeared to break up unexpectedly. Sometime around the end of July, the Chinese reconnaissance satellite Yaogan 50-02 , which had only been launched some four months earlier, also broke up in orbit. On Sept. 13, a similar fate befell the U.S. Cold War-era Farrah III spy satellite , also known as USA 32. At the time of writing, no firm evidence has emerged to indicate any of these incidents were the result of hostile action rather than accidents of some kind. ”
Directed energy attacks, in particular, from one satellite against another, may be very hard to attribute as they can happen over longer distances in the vacuum of space. They would also presumably allow the attacking satellite to engage multiple targets, even in a relatively short period of time, making it one of the most attractive potential anti-satellite capabilities on orbit.
In addition to talking about Chinese space-based ASAT capabilities, the DIA report raised concerns about a wide array of threats from the PLA as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran.
The report did not address Russian space-based directed energy weapons plans. However, it did note that, like China, Russia does have ground-based laser systems already capable of affecting U.S. and allied satellites. The threat from these systems is not theoretical. They are part of an array of ASAT measures that China and Russia have used against the U.S. for years.

articles.title_orig: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
Carney backs EU-Canada associate membership amid Trump tariff threats
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies , which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “ associate member ” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
At least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened.
As well as those killed, 50 people were also injured, the minister said.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported .
The local Castilla-La Mancha government confirmed at least 68 people had died, higher than another high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people in January.
Emiliano García-Page, the president of the region, said 24 people had died on a train operated by rail company Renfe, with the rest killed on a train operated by Iryo.
More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, newspaper El País said.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe train, saying the cause was "still unknown".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"If there has been any negligence, it will come to light," he later said at a press conference.
"If there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. It is clear that we have experienced two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail within the same year."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election on Nov. 29, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.
