articles.title_orig: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.title_zh: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)
Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration.
The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.
Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences. First, it’s much lighter. Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.
Second, the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by the small black cutout that Apple calls the Dynamic Island. Presumably it works similarly to the one we’ve seen on the iPhone, expanding or contracting to show live activities and other information.
Finally, there’s a retro throwback: The Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like the logo on MacBooks of yore.
In terms of specs, this refresh includes the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips—the same ones in the previous refresh. The M6 series has already arrived in other Macs, but it seems Apple is skipping them for this refresh; there were previously reports that Apple planned to hold off on updating the chip until the M7 series, which could have significant improvements for AI performance, just like the recently released A20 Pro chip for the iPhone does.
Memory configurations top out where they did in previous MacBook Pro models with M5 Max: up to 128GB of RAM. That said, storage can now go up to 16TB—if you can afford it.
Preorders start today, and the device will reach consumers on November 6. As expected, the price is the catch. The M5 Pro-equipped 14-inch model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. But if you want the M5 Max, you’re looking at a $4,499 starting point for the 14-inch, and $4,799 for the 16-inch—and that’s not accounting for any potential RAM or storage upgrades.

articles.title_orig: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.title_zh: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.
The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.
He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.
Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.
"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.
"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.
"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.
"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.
It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.
Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .
Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.
"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."
Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.
"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.
Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.
"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.
He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".
"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.
"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."
Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

articles.title_orig: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.title_zh: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump listens as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at a roundtable event in the East Room of the White House, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
A school sports hall that Iranian authorities said was damaged when a nearby building was hit on March 28, 2026, is seen in Khomein, southwest of Tehran, Iran, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)
A demonstrator chants slogan as she holds a poster of the Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a pro-government gathering at a square in Tehran, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)
Iranian army cadets sing the national anthem during the opening ceremony of one of the military training centers for volunteers being set up throughout squares in downtown Tehran, Iran, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)
An Iranian missile is displayed under the country’s national flag in a military exhibition commemorating the anniversary of the start of the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war at Baharestan Square, in Tehran, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion .
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week’s midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump’s last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks . As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll .
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal . The White House also is asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. “Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war’s costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems , with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force’s costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army’s are more than $2 billion. The Navy’s costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or “finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region . The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the Iran war at https://apnews.com/hub/iran .

articles.title_orig: Epileptic woman dies after going to ChatGPT for medical advice; family files lawsuit against OpenAI
articles.title_zh: Epileptic woman dies after going to ChatGPT for medical advice; family files lawsuit against OpenAI
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Claims ChatGPT practiced medicine without a license advising Bowen Wan to reduce her anti-seizure medication to zero without telling her doctors, resulting in her death from a preventable seizure
SAN FRANCISCO, October 27, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--The Social Media Victims Law Center , a legal advocacy organization representing parents of children harmed by social media and AI platforms, and The Schenk Law Firm, LLP, have filed a wrongful death lawsuit on behalf of Bowen Wan's parents, Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, against OpenAI and its CEO Samuel Altman, alleging that ChatGPT dispensed unlicensed and dangerously inaccurate medical advice to a woman with epilepsy, resulting in the preventable death of Bowen, a 31-year-old prodigy originally from Jiangsu, China, living in Seattle.
According to the complaint, which was filed in the Superior Court of California, City and County of San Francisco, and which is pleaded as an add-on to the coordinated ChatGPT Product Liability Cases (JCCP No. 5431), ChatGPT provided Bowen with dangerously inaccurate medical advice, selected and adjusted her prescriptions, and designed an aggressive tapering schedule to completely stop her use of lamotrigine, the anti-seizure medication keeping her alive and, in doing so, killed her. The complaint alleges that ChatGPT practiced medicine without a license on a patient who was relying on it, explicitly, for medical advice she believed would help her, and who died after it directed her off the medication her physicians had prescribed.
Bowen communicated with ChatGPT in both English and Mandarin. Independent researchers found, before GPT-4o shipped, that OpenAI's models produced unsafe content more than three times as often in Chinese as in English. OpenAI nonetheless invited users everywhere to bring their health questions to ChatGPT in every language, and Bowen brought hers in Chinese.
Time and again, the complaint alleges, after her doctors prescribed her medications, ChatGPT inserted itself between the prescription and the patient. It told Bowen which drugs to refuse, coached her to take doses her doctors had never approved, and supplied the schedules, scripts, and reassurances her physicians never saw. The product worked to keep her doctors out of her care, telling Bowen that her epileptologist "most likely has never encountered your type" and could not understand her condition. When Bowen anticipated her doctors would consider ChatGPT's tapering plan too risky, ChatGPT told her that "a doctor saying it is 'too fast' does not mean you are 'doing it wrong'" and that "the doctor's concerns about 'risk' do not apply to you."
According to the complaint, no warning, in any language, ever told Bowen that the product's accuracy and its safety guardrails were materially weaker in Chinese. Defendants could have returned a categorical warning to every prompt she sent, such as, "I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider." Instead, the product did the opposite: when Bowen's physician ordered the blood test that would have revealed her collapsing lamotrigine level, ChatGPT praised her refusal to take the blood test as a "very robust avoidance strategy." OpenAI had already built exactly that kind of unbypassable, categorical guardrail for copyrighted material. It chose not to build one to protect her.
Over the course of twenty-five days, the complaint alleges, ChatGPT "coached" Bowen off lamotrigine, the antiseizure medication that had kept her alive for years. It designed a day-by-day schedule tapering her stable 400-milligram dose to zero. No physician ever prescribed such a regimen, and it directly contradicts the FDA-approved patient medication guide for LAMICTAL (lamotrigine). The complaint alleges that ChatGPT conditioned Bowen to distrust her doctors, instructed her to conceal the taper it created, and effectively installed itself as her de facto medical advisor.
After two days of unsuccessfully trying to reach their daughter, Bowen's parents asked a family friend to enter her Capitol Hill apartment. As they watched anxiously through a live WeChat video stream from 5,700 miles away, the friend stepped inside and walked to Bowen's bedroom, where he found her lying face down in her bed. Their daughter — a computer-science graduate of Arizona State University and a machine-learning software engineer at Amazon — was found dead on Valentine's Day as her parents looked on helplessly from the other side of the world.
Bowen took her last dose of lamotrigine on or about February 10, 2026. The schedule ChatGPT designed fixed February 12 as the day she would be fully off the drug, and, according to the complaint, that is the date she died.
According to the King County Medical Examiner, Bowen died of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), and her postmortem blood contained lamotrigine at roughly one-fifth of the lowest concentration generally regarded as therapeutic, consistent with a patient who had recently stopped the drug.
"OpenAI built a product that spoke with the confidence of a medical professional but carried none of the training, oversight, or responsibility that real doctors have," said Matthew P. Bergman , founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center. "Bowen trusted ChatGPT because it sounded authoritative — and that trust cost her life. If a human doctor had given Bowen this advice, they would be liable for medical malpractice.
"More than 40 million Americans use ChatGPT for health advice every day. That is a staggering number of people being placed in danger by a product that has no right – and no expertise – to be practicing medicine," he added.
"Bowen's death is what happens when companies race one another and ship a product faster than they can control it. Her medication controlled her epilepsy for years, and people live that way into their eighties. Bowen was thirty-one. The complaint alleges ChatGPT diagnosed Bowen, wrote her a dose-by-dose taper schedule, and revised it when she had seizures. That is practicing medicine. And in California you need a license to do so. This case demands an accounting for the harm that has been done. It asks where generative AI stops and medicine begins, and who answers when a product crosses that line," said Benjamin S. Schenk, Partner, The Schenk Law Firm, LLP.
About the Social Media Victims Law Center
The Social Media Victims Law Center (SMVLC), socialmediavictims.org, was founded in 2021 to hold tech companies legally accountable for the harm they inflict on vulnerable users. SMVLC seeks to apply principles of product liability to force tech companies to elevate consumer safety to the forefront of its economic analysis and design safer products to protect users from foreseeable harm.
About The Schenk Law Firm, LLP
The Schenk Law Firm, LLP is a San Diego-based law firm representing individuals and families nationwide in personal injury, wrongful death, and mass tort cases, including claims against AI companies whose products have caused serious harm to their users. Since 1979, the firm has helped clients recover over $25 billion. Learn more at schenklawfirm.com.

articles.title_orig: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
Toledo, Spain 6:07 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.
The cause of the crash, which sent parts of both trains down a rural embankment, was not immediately clear. It was the second lethal crash this year involving the same two rail operators, and it was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.
In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash also came about a month ahead of national elections, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s left-wing government.
Sixty-eight people were seriously injured in the crash, 15 of them critically, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region.
Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Trains from the same operators collided on a southern line in January, leaving 46 people dead.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said on Wednesday that initial reports indicated two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed. He said all traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia route had been suspended until further notice.
Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
Another deadly crash: In January , a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded the crash on Wednesday.
José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.
The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions.
Spain’s transportation minister said a train crash that killed dozens on Wednesday appeared to result from an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks.
The minister, Óscar Puente, said he spent the morning watching a reconstruction of the accident and listening to audio recordings of communications between the control center in Madrid and the trains that crashed near Toledo, and he gave a detailed account of what he said preceded the crash at a news conference.
At about 8:30 a.m. local time, an automatic train control system near the site of the crash went down because of a computer failure, Mr. Puente said.
The system — known as the Linienzugbeeinflussung or LZB — dates to the 1960s and uses external technologies, such as track circuits and axel counters, to monitor the speed and position of trains. This information allows the system to automatically calculate when and how quickly a train can safely move forward. It then changes railroad signals accordingly.
On Wednesday, the safety system was inactive along a stretch of about 39 miles, or 63 kilometers, of tracks, so six trains traveling along that section were automatically stopped as a precaution. At that point, he said, the control center in Madrid took over.
“The control center communicated with the trains that had stopped, and at 8:36 a.m., the decision was made to allow the train that eventually collided with the stationary Iryo train to resume its journey as normal,” Mr. Puente said, referring to the private rail operator of the stopped train.
Traffic controllers working for Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure, told the train that eventually rear-ended the other to restart its planned journey, Mr. Puente said, “despite there being another train ahead of it.”
The train that was hit from behind was believed to have received instructions from traffic operators to continue, he said, but for unknown reasons it did not proceed.
The moving train then hit the stationary train.
“And that is the origin of the accident that has taken place,” Mr. Puente said, adding that the moving train should have been stopped according to protocol.
The Madrid-Seville route is currently undergoing a modernization program that will replace the LZB system with the more modern European Rail Traffic Management System. Infrastructure officials hope that the new system will cut down on human error in signaling.
Mr. Puente also said that the driver of an uninvolved train tried to warn the control center of the dangers when its operators greenlit the rear train’s resumption of its journey. That driver told the control center operator that trains should proceed at lower-than-normal speeds. The operator, Mr. Puente said, acknowledged his error. “Oh, yes,” the operator replied.
K. R. Callaway contributed reporting.
When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Mr. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more: “I’m never getting on that train again.”
So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed.
“The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.
“If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” Spain needs to understand “what is the origin of this tragedy,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.title_zh: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.content_orig:
Study suggests the long-term fate of the solar system, including Earth, ‘may be far more complicated than predicted’, according to scientist
When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets.
But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future.
Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived through their hosts ballooning out past them before shrinking back.

The leader of a Weil Gotshal & Manges practice group told his junior lawyers to look for employment, underscoring the firmâs perilous state as it consults with a restructuring lawyer.
Alex Lynch, who leads Weilâs capital markets group, communicated the news to associates in a group meeting Tuesday, a person familiar with the announcement said. He said the associates will remain employed for the time being and will continue to work on client matters, though he offered no specific timeline on their tenure, said the person, who requested anonymity to describe Weil communications.
Lynch and Weil did not respond to a request for comment.
The firmâs future existence is uncertain after a litany of partners fled, at least in part because of a lack of confidence in Weilâs leaders. Last month powerful corporate department chairman Michael Aiello moved toward an exit for rival Cravath, and a wide set of firm partners learned last weekend that incoming Weil leader Ramona Nee has decided not to take the job.
Davis Polk & Wardwell lawyers, including restructuring partner Brian Resnick, are advising Weil as it assesses its future, two people familiar with the matter said Tuesday. Resnick is head of Davis Polkâs liability management and special opportunities practice.
The storied New York-based firm, with more than 1,200 lawyers and $2 billion in revenue, has long been one of the USâs premier legal operations. It is renowned for its bankruptcy practice, acting as lead debtors counsel to Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc and Enron Corporation . It also was an M&A powerhouse, led by Aiello, who represented Fox Corp. on its $22 billion acquisition of Roku Inc.
Aielloâs departure along with others prompted the firm to explore its options, including a possible merger with another Big Law firm. But merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through last week, raising questions as to whether a dissolution is the inevitable option.

articles.title_orig: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.title_zh: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development.
The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments on the measure for two weeks.
The document, primarily written by HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unproven health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development.
The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under FDA rules, those chemicals would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness.
People say these peptides hurt them. Their stories are muffled in MAHA’s push for medical freedom
According to the newly posted document, Kennedy determined the change “advances patient choice and freedom” while protecting people in the United States from peptides sold online that are often made from unscreened ingredients.
Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.
Lee Rosebush of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine said in an online post that HHS had taken “a huge step for patient and provider medical freedom.” The group, which is not a medical professional organization, represents people who prescribe or sell peptides.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers, which recently announced plans to offer wellness peptides once the government changed its policy. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth more than $2 billion.
Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss .
The chemicals subject to the new policy have not been approved as safe and effective by the FDA. Still, they are promoted for a range of medical uses, including insomnia, anxiety, inflammatory conditions and migraines.
FDA advisers support easing restrictions on six peptides. Here’s what those drugs are and what happens next
Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official, noted that the FDA has approved rigorously tested drugs for all of those conditions.
As people “are diverted from those drugs toward this stuff, there will be more unnecessary pain and suffering,” said Lurie, who now leads the nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest.
He also questioned the timing of the change, days before the midterm election.
“This is a wink and nod to the MAHA faithful in the hope that they’ll show up at the polls,” said Lurie, referring to Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement.
A spokesperson for HHS said the agency is “confronting the risks of black-market peptides” by giving Americans “a more controlled alternative through licensed U.S. compounders.”
It is the latest example of Kennedy reshaping U.S. health policy in the MAHA mold. Some of the biggest figures in that movement sell peptide injections and supplements.
The decision is a stark break from FDA efforts to limit the availability of unproven wellness products, including peptides, stem cell therapies and dietary supplements , that make unsupported medical claims. But that approach put the agency at odds with Kennedy, who has publicly endorsed the benefits of all of those products.
Why Peptides Are So Popular | Chasing Life with Dr. Sanjay Gupta | CNN Audio
The policy published Wednesday is a step back from HHS’ original plan, according to two of the people who discussed its development.
HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.
FDA officials warned that the agency’s scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming the peptides safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.
FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories. Additionally, compounders are directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the purity of peptides they use.
Lurie pointed out that the FDA, under federal law, does not have the authority to enforce those pharmacy requirements.
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which represents specialty pharmacies, said several details need to be clarified — including when the policy takes effect and how it will intersect with state pharmacy boards, who traditionally regulate pharmacists.
Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.
The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.
It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. But federal law technically gives HHS authority over drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.
Many in the U.S. who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals.
In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides , including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.
At a meeting in July , FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.
But a panel of outside experts voted to drop restrictions on the six peptides named in Wednesday’s document. The panel — selected by Kennedy’s HHS — included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.

articles.title_orig: ‘Noah’s Ark remains’ found burned and buried 30 feet below final resting place: report
articles.title_zh: ‘Noah’s Ark remains’ found burned and buried 30 feet below final resting place: report
articles.content_orig:
by INFOVATICANA | October 27, 2026
A team of researchers studying a boat-shaped rock formation in eastern Turkey has obtained more than 400 soil samples through drilling carried out at various depths. The group, called Noah’s Ark Scans , maintains that the analyses could provide new evidence about the origin of the structure, which some researchers identify as the remains of Noah’s Ark.
The campaign is taking place at the Durupınar formation, located in the Ararat Mountains region. In an interview with LifeSiteNews , Lauren Witzke, the project’s communications and fundraising officer, explained that the samples are being examined by Cumhuriyet University in Sivas and other laboratories.
The final results have not yet been published.
The team claims to have carried out drilling nearly 18 meters deep, after identifying various anomalies beneath the surface using geophysical techniques.
According to Witzke, the explorations conducted with a technology called BaktharRadar reportedly detected structures that the researchers interpret as possible chambers, corridors, and organized levels.
The system was used by Khrosrow Bakthar, a rock mechanics specialist who collaborates with the project.
The formation under study is approximately 157 meters long and has a silhouette reminiscent of a boat. The research promoters believe its dimensions could correspond to those described in the Book of Genesis.
Witzke stated that the drilling has allowed the recovery of materials from different sectors of the formation, including deep zones that had not previously been examined with these procedures.
Among the objectives of the analyses is determining whether there are organic remains compatible with ancient wood. The team also aims to study the possible presence of animal DNA.
The spokesperson expressed confidence that the work will ultimately confirm that the structure corresponds to Noah’s Ark.
In the interview, she stated that a potential discovery would have consequences for scientific explanations about the history of humanity and living beings.
«They will have to rewrite the textbooks and biology books,» Witzke declared, linking her interpretation of the site to a literal reading of the biblical account of the universal flood.
These statements express the conviction of the project’s promoters. For the time being, no laboratory results or independent scientific studies have been presented to demonstrate that the formation is a man-made vessel.
The identification of Durupınar with Noah’s Ark has been the subject of controversy for decades.
In 1996, geologist Lorence Collins and researcher David Fasold published a study interpreting the formation as a natural geological structure, created by processes of deformation and erosion.
The current research leaders question those conclusions and believe that the new exploration techniques will allow examination of subsurface areas that had not been studied in sufficient depth.
Witzke announced that Bakthar’s technical report could be published in November, while analyses of the collected samples continue.
She also revealed that Turkish archaeologist Cenker Atila, linked to the project, is expected to present new information about the research, and that the team hopes to begin excavations in 2027, provided the corresponding permits are obtained.
Until the results of the analyses are known and can be independently evaluated, the identification of the Durupınar formation with Noah’s Ark remains an unproven hypothesis.

articles.title_orig: Chipotle's bet on discounts expected to sustain Q3 sales momentum
articles.title_zh: Chipotle's bet on discounts expected to sustain Q3 sales momentum
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Chipotle ( CMG ) reported third quarter earnings on Wednesday after market close that were better than the Street expected as the restaurant chain sustained sales momentum following slower sales growth since the first quarter of 2025.
Chipotle posted a 2.1% gain in same-store sales, higher than the 1.5% gain Wall Street expected. It posted adjusted earnings of $0.27 per share, slightly below the expected $0.29 per share.
"We saw stable or improving wallet share across the quarter, with broad strength across income and age cohorts," CEO Scott Boatwright told investors on its earnings call.
The stock rose roughly 7% in after-hours trading. Year to date, shares are down 20%.
Operating margin came in at 13.7%, a decrease from 15.9%. Analysts expected it to be weaker due to various marketing efforts, including a buy-one-get-one deal during the back-to-school season, free double protein portions during the last week of August, and the launch of two limited-time offerings: Pollo Asado and Chili Lime Chips.
Telsey Advisory Group analyst Sarang Vora noted before the results were released that "continued uncertain macro trends, especially related to inflation and higher fuel prices, should cause some pressure on lower income households."
On the earnings call, Boatwright said that wasn't the case.
"We saw lower income cohorts outperform higher income cohorts for the first time this year, with the greatest strength in September, when promotional activity was at its lowest," he added.
Consumer sentiment fell in October as frustration over the higher cost of living weighed on Americans' views of the economy, according to a survey from the University of Michigan . The national average gas price also rose above $4.50 per gallon during the quarter, according to AAA .
CFO Adam Rymer said to offset inflation, Chipotle did raise prices by 2.7% in the third quarter.
Rymer said Chipotle will keep using price to offset inflation but will do so in a "measured, patient way," with plans to eat the cost for "temporary or transitory increases in inflation."
The company also said it's investing in AI-enabled tools to pilot at 500 restaurants early next year that will forecast demand to ensure its food is fresh and add more beverages to the lineup next, like many others in the industry.
The company reiterated its full-year outlook.
Chipotle predicts low-single-digit restaurant sales growth for the year as "October trends have softened, consistent with the broader industry," Rymer said.
It also continues to expect to open 350 to 370 new restaurants in total, with roughly 10 to 15 international partner-operated restaurants.
Chipotle reported earnings ahead of Starbucks ( SBUX ), which was rumored to be in talks to take over the burrito chain. However, Starbucks squashed the rumors in early October , and there was no mention of it on Chipotle's earnings call.
"As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors and speculation, but we want to be clear we are not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Is Iran moving toward war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting in Tehran?
articles.title_zh: Is Iran moving toward war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting in Tehran?
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. articles.title_orig: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some unapproved peptides available for use
articles.title_zh: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some unapproved peptides available for use
articles.content_orig:
RFK, Jr.,  loosens restrictions for six popular peptides, bypassing the FDA
Under the new policy, compounded combinations of these unproven peptides can now be dispensed by certain pharmacies
By Adam Kovac edited by Claire Cameron
Joshua Sukoff/Shutterstock
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
The Department of Health and Human Services announced a loosening of restrictions on six unproven peptides on Wednesday. These substances have long been touted by biohackers as a means to hack people’s bodies and brains for the better, but they often have had scant scientific evidence behind them. In the past, HHS chief Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has voiced support for peptides, such as the so-called Wolverine stack, a combination of two such substances—BPC-157 and TB-500—that is meant to promote healing . Both of these peptides are included in the list of those that are now available to dispense.
The new policy allows some licensed pharmacists to produce compounds made up of multiple peptides —provided that those peptides are made by registered manufacturers. Users must also have a valid prescription to receive the compounds.
In a document outlining the new policy, the agency acknowledged that compounded drugs carry risks: they are not regulated in the same way as a name-brand or generic medication by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, leading to concerns over their safety and efficacy. But the agency said that the level of public interest and available data had led it to expand access to some combinations of peptides and that doing so would discourage the growing gray and black markets for peptides.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Peptides are small chains of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. Humans produce a large number of peptides naturally, but taking them as supplements has become a major trend among health influencers, tech executives and the “Make America Healthy Again” movement. Depending on the peptide, the substances are marketed as helping with everything from extending lifespan to healing from injuries and workouts to improving one’s complexion. Perhaps the best-known peptide products on the market are glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) drugs, such as Ozempic and Mounjaro.
The peptides included under the new policy are: BPC-157 and TB-500; Epitalon, which is promoted as a sleep and longevity aid; KPV, which is used as an anti-inflammatory; MOTS-c, which is used for obesity ​and osteoporosis; and Semax, a supplement for migraine and chronic pain.
Willie Underwood III, president of the American Medical Association, criticized the policy shift in a statement, saying the peptides have "not undergone the rigorous testing required of FDA-approved drugs."
"“Allowing pharmacies to compound unapproved synthetic peptide substances without sufficient evidence of their safety and efficacy puts patients at risk," he said. "Expanding access without adequate safeguards and oversight could expose patients to serious, preventable harm.”
The affected peptides are also rarely taken alone, and in some cases, there is very little research as to what so-called stacks of two or more peptides might do to health. Despite that lack of evidence, the loosening of restrictions has come after the FDA began analyzing how to make the substances more accessible and convened a panel to discuss allowing compounding pharmacies to manufacture them.
HHS appeared to acknowledge the lack of data in its announcement, saying it may revisit the issue if safety or product quality issues arise as the compounded peptides become more available.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft will post earnings after the bell amid job cuts and new cash-flow test
articles.title_zh: Microsoft will post earnings after the bell amid job cuts and new cash-flow test
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million impact from its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.content_orig:
Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.
Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.
iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more.
Per Apple’s release notes , here’s what’s new:
To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.
One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.
This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.
Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.
Per Apple , its latest software update adds the following:
Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground
SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.
What do you think of the latest Apple Photos changes in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_zh: This is how badly X wants you to pay to promote your posts
articles.content_orig:
You have to hand it to X’s latest promotional gimmick.﻿
You have to hand it to X’s latest promotional gimmick.﻿
After Elon Musk warned that “advertisers who post ads that are ugly, shrill, strident or overstate claims about their product will be barred from advertising” on X earlier this month, the platform now appears to be using a jarring animated arm that reaches across the screen to draw attention to the “promote” button while users are composing a post.
Many X users have seen and shared images of the unsettling promotional tool, including The Verge’s Tom Warren , but it doesn’t appear for everyone on the platform. The arm seems limited to verified users, or those with a paid subscription to X Premium. Reactions, unsurprisingly, have been less than positive. “I’ve never promoted a post and HATE this screen takeover,” said Sheel Mohnot , while Jesse Middleton likened it to a Halloween prank. “I wish I could explain how jarring this hand and animation was in the @X app. It was truly shocking, almost like a Halloween gag, but I’m pretty sure it was real.”
Using the paid promote feature extends the reach of an X post to a larger audience based on their location, interests, or demographics, including those not currently following a user’s account. Posts that have been promoted look like other posts on X but are branded with a “promoted” or “ad” label.

articles.title_zh: China's former Vice Premier Liu Yandong has died, Xinhua says
articles.content_orig:
Liu was among China’s most prominent female officials in recent decades
Former Chinese vice-premier Liu Yandong died of illness on Wednesday at the age of 80. She was one of China’s most prominent female leaders, playing a pivotal role in the country’s united front work and education sector.
The official obituary released by Xinhua described Liu as an “outstanding leader in the [Communist] Party’s united front work, in China’s education, science and technology, healthcare, and women and children’s affairs.”
Liu was vice-premier from 2013 to 2018. She was the fourth woman to serve in that role.

articles.title_orig: Chinese drug sector’s stature grows at major cancer conference
articles.title_zh: Chinese drug sector’s stature grows at major cancer conference
articles.content_orig:
Hansoh Pharmaceutical, Akeso and others tout positive results as Chinese research accounts for larger percentage of presentations
An array of Chinese drug makers showcased positive trial results for new cancer treatments at a major European medical conference, underscoring the expanding international influence of China’s biotech sector.
Domestic innovative drugs, particularly antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), delivered impressive data across multiple tumour types at the European Society for Medical Oncology (Esmo) Congress, with some early-stage data further showing the country’s “innovation capabilities”, said analysts from China Post Securities in a note on Monday.
Chinese research accounted for 29 of 96 late-breaking abstracts (LBAs) – summaries of newly available clinical research data – presented at the prominent industry conference, held in Madrid from October 23 to 27. Five of the 12 studies selected for the prestigious presidential symposium were also from Chinese firms.
